## TL;DR

Linux user services now receive the PATH from the shell that runs `repoos service install`, which allows agent CLIs installed in user directories such as `~/.local/bin` to be found later by systemd. Before writing a Linux unit, installation checks that each enabled, explicitly configured agent CLI resolves on that PATH and returns a direct remediation message if it does not. An asynchronous `spawn` failure with code `ENOENT` is now recorded as a readable system transcript line naming the command and the PATH searched, so the task’s existing dev-error escalation includes useful context instead of an empty log.

The macOS LaunchAgent already had a PATH environment variable sourced from the installing process, so its service configuration did not need a change. I added tests for Linux unit PATH generation and the ENOENT classifier, including a non-ENOENT control case. The required `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed after formatting and the Cursor executable mapping correction. The final remote run passed the build and 248 scoped/always-run test files (4,004 passed, 1 skipped); local format, lint, build, UI smoke, and rendered contrast guards also passed. An intermediate post-format attempt exited 255 during remote tests without emitting test output; a retry passed, and the final check after the mapping correction passed as well.

## Work and rationale

Inspection of `src/core/service-manager.ts` confirmed that `generatePlist()` already writes `process.env.PATH` under `EnvironmentVariables`, while `generateUnit()` wrote no environment assignment at all. systemd user units do not inherit the shell environment that invoked installation. This is enough to explain why a CLI that worked interactively could disappear after service installation. Unit generation now emits a quoted `Environment="PATH=..."` assignment from the current PATH, with systemd-sensitive percent signs doubled and quotes/backslashes escaped. The fallback remains a conventional system executable PATH for environments where PATH is unset.

The install path validates enabled entries in the repository’s explicit `agents` configuration against the same PATH that will be written to systemd. Existing CLI names whose executable differs from the configuration label are mapped to their executable names (`claude`, `copilot`, `qwen`, `agy`, and `kiro-cli`); names that already represent an executable are checked as-is. The check uses `which` with the candidate PATH and returns `{ ok: false }` with the missing executable and corrective guidance before writing the unit. The scope stays Linux-only because launchd already preserves PATH.

The launch failure has two forms in this code: a synchronous throw from `spawn`, already logged and emitted, and the usual asynchronous ChildProcess `error` event, which previously triggered cleanup without carrying the error into the task transcript. The asynchronous handler now classifies ENOENT, records a system line containing the missing command and current PATH, and logs the same detail. Existing cleanup and dev-error escalation then persist that line into the task’s needs-input detail. Other spawn error codes keep their existing handling.

## Approaches tried

I followed the service code from unit generation through `installService`, then compared it with the adjacent plist generator. I followed the agent process lifecycle from `spawn` through the `error` listener, cleanup, and task failure escalation. This kept the fix at the relevant boundaries: Linux service generation/install validation and the runner’s spawn-error event. I added a small pure classifier so ENOENT behavior can be tested without launching a real missing executable.

## Challenges and blockers

The repository has no focused agent-runner test module named for `agents.ts`, so I placed the classification helper and test in `src/core`, and wired the runner to that helper. The Linux service generator uses the installed RepoOS executable resolution helper, so the unit-generation test exercises that existing prerequisite as well as checking the generated PATH line. This host is not the affected ThinkPad; the patch does not claim live Linux/systemd verification. The task does not require a device test, and none was performed.

## Key learnings

launchd and systemd differ in whether they receive a useful user PATH by default. The launchd plist already addressed this explicitly, while a systemd user unit needs an `Environment=` setting. Also, missing executable failures normally arrive asynchronously as ChildProcess `error` events; if that handler discards the error, durable stdout/stderr files can remain empty even though the task eventually receives a generic failure state. Capturing the command and searched PATH at that boundary makes the existing failure flow actionable.
